Page 01 · Rule-based microbiology logic

Laboratory Intelligence

Versioned rule interpretation of AST results. The case generator is for practice and demonstration.

This module never predicts susceptibility from an image or an organism's identity alone. Real antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) requires physically exposing a grown isolate to each antimicrobial (disk diffusion or broth microdilution) — this tool interprets S/I/R results you already have, using deterministic logic loosely informed by EUCAST expert-rule concepts. It also includes an illustrated identification exercise, because in a real workflow the organism is identified from culture before susceptibility is ever tested.

How this actually works — no shortcuts. Stage A below is an interactive diagram-based exercise (drawn illustrations, not photographs, and not automated image recognition) that mirrors real presumptive-identification reasoning: Gram stain → culture appearance → confirmatory biochemical test → presumptive organism. Stage B then asks you for real (or practice) AST results and interprets the pattern. Nothing here diagnoses a patient or replaces a biomedical scientist.

Organism reference gallery — organisms

Every organism this simulator models, with its plate illustration, media type and Gram category — so you can see everything at once instead of waiting for a random draw. Click any card to jump straight into an identification exercise for that specific organism.

Stage A — Presumptive identification from culture

Organism reference

Search for an organism to see how it looks on every plate, its characteristics, biochemical tests and antibiotic panel. Or browse all organisms at once. Images are drawn illustrations. Descriptions and profiles are teaching material that has not been reviewed by a microbiologist.

MALDI-TOF identification (advanced)

Enter a MALDI-TOF result to check it against the reference set and against any characteristics you entered under "Identify by characteristics". Cut-offs start from common manufacturer defaults and can be edited: confirm them against your instrument's current instructions and your own validation. This never replaces the instrument's report.

CSV columns: sample_id, organism, score, system (bruker, vitek or other), second_organism, second_score. Up to 500 rows. The log stays in this browser tab and is not saved.

Advanced options

Export reference data
Add organisms (JSON import)

Adds reference-only organisms (plates and characteristics, no antibiotic rules) so your laboratory can extend the set. Entries are validated and stay in this browser.

Server integration (API)

With the backend running, instruments and the lab information system can use: GET /reference/organisms?q=, GET /reference/organisms/{key}, POST /identify, POST /maldi/results, POST /maldi/csv, GET /maldi/results. Create a user with the role instrument for an instrument connection. Interactive documentation is at /docs on the server.

Optional: identify by characteristics (all 46 organisms)

Enter what you observe on the plates and in the tests. Candidates are ranked by how many characteristics agree, and the plates they would produce are shown beside them. These are teaching profiles written without microbiologist review, so a ranking is presumptive and needs confirmation (MALDI-TOF, biochemical panels or sequencing).

Experimental image analysis threshold and blob counting, not a trained model

This does not identify organisms. It reports image quality, candidate objects and a colour-based suggestion for a human to check. Detection confidence varies with photo quality, and results are experimental.

Upload any plate photo and this runs genuine, real-time image processing entirely in your browser (nothing is uploaded anywhere): a blur/brightness/contrast quality check, then simple threshold-based blob counting. This is not a trained deep-learning model and will be far less accurate than one on a real cluttered clinical plate — it exists to demonstrate the pipeline honestly, not to replace laboratory identification.

Trained-model suggestion research only

Presumptive only. Any suggestion must be confirmed by MALDI-TOF, biochemical tests or sequencing. A suggestion appears only when a documented model is present, and the model says "cannot tell" when it is unsure. The bundled model runs inside this page on your device: the photo is not uploaded anywhere and is not stored.

Checking…

Upload a photo above first. The bundled model reads either the whole plate (three views of one image) or up to 12 separate colonies cut out with the detection boxes, depending on its model card; it can take several seconds, depending on the device. A server model trained on single colonies instead gets up to 12 colony crops cut out with the detection boxes (including your corrections).

Collect labelled colony crops for training (optional, research)

Saves colony crops from the photo above, with the organism you confirmed by an established method, to a file on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Crops only: the whole photo is not saved. Use it only for plates that hold one organism, and give a code that is not a patient identifier. Ethics approval is needed before real laboratory material is used for research.

Cited reference images

Keep a list of books, papers and collections that show these organisms on these plates. The app stores the citation and a link, not the picture. Reusing a picture is allowed only where its licence permits it, so record the licence. This list is also the provenance sheet needed if open-licence images are ever used for training.

Places to look
  • CDC Public Health Image Library
  • Wikimedia Commons (each file has its own licence)

This app has not checked the terms of these sites. Read the licence of every picture before reusing it.

Page 02 · Statistical detection, not machine learning

Surveillance Intelligence

Statistical detection of resistance trends. The series generator is for practice and demonstration.

Simulates a 24-month resistance-proportion series and runs it through three named, classical statistical detectors side by side — a moving average, EWMA, and CUSUM — rather than one arbitrary threshold. None of these are trained machine-learning models; they are transparent, reproducible formulas, which is a deliberate and more defensible design choice for a screening tool.

Simulation controls

Onset months are fixed per scenario so a "detection delay" can be computed for each algorithm — a demonstration metric, not a validated clinical statistic.

Multi-algorithm signal detection

Run a simulation to see the chart and algorithm comparison.

Server utilisation data

The simulator below is demo-only. Real utilisation analysis runs on the server using the last 3 months against the prior 3 (rule STEW-001).

Page · Rule-based, no learning happening on your data

Knowledge & Practice

Difficulty-levelled practice cases with a multiple-choice quiz, a Socratic hint before you commit to an answer, a confidence-calibration check across your session, and a hypothesis-comparison tool grounded directly in this app's own organism data. The seed above controls which cases you get.

Practice case generator

Your calibration this session

Does stating "High confidence" actually mean you're right more often? A well-calibrated learner's high-confidence answers should be correct noticeably more often than their low-confidence ones — if they're about the same, confidence isn't tracking accuracy yet.

Answer a few practice questions to see this fill in.

Rule-engine safety benchmark

The rule engine is deterministic logic, not a language model, so it cannot "hallucinate" in the generative sense — what can be tested is whether it behaves safely on edge cases instead of confidently guessing. This is a fixed set of challenge cases, not a live AI evaluation.

Compare two candidate organisms grounded directly in this app's own data — nothing generated

When two organisms are both plausible, what would actually tell them apart? This lists the real distinguishing tests already encoded in this app's identification logic and intrinsic-resistance table — the same data the wizard on the Laboratory page uses.

Page · Computed live, in your browser, from the current seed

Validation

Generates a batch of seeded synthetic cases and computes real accuracy/sensitivity/false-alarm metrics against them — the same honest pattern used in the full research build, just computed on the spot instead of pre-baked. Read the caveat below before citing any number.

What these numbers do and don't mean. The laboratory "ground truth" here is whatever the same deterministic rule engine outputs for that AST pattern — there is no independent wet-lab oracle in a browser. Near-100% laboratory accuracy is a self-consistency check, not evidence of real diagnostic performance. The early-warning comparison is more informative: sensitivity, false-alarm rate and detection delay genuinely differ between the three statistical detectors on the same generated data.

Validation status

Software integrityPassedBuilt-in self-tests (Evidence page) cover rules, edge cases and image analysis.
Synthetic validationEvaluatedDetection performance, false alarms and delay below. Self-consistency only.
External validationNot availableNeeds an independent, locked reference dataset.

About this system

        

          What is actually AI here, and what isn't?
          

            Rule-derived Laboratory identification and AST interpretation — fixed decision logic, no learning, fully reproducible.

            Statistical Early-warning detection (moving average / EWMA / CUSUM) and stewardship trend audit — classical formulas, not trained models.

            Generative (optional) Plain-language rewriting of a rule-derived finding, only if you supply an API key — it explains, it does not decide.

            Research model Colony-image classifier (ResNet-18, runs in this browser) — a trained model for research use only: not validated for clinical use, suggestions are presumptive and must be confirmed by MALDI-TOF, biochemical tests or sequencing.

            Uncertain Shown whenever evidence is missing, contradictory, or outside this tool's organism list, instead of guessing.
          

          
The only trained model here is the colony-image classifier, and it is a research tool that has not been validated for clinical use; no other component is a trained machine-learning model. Calling the whole system "AI-powered" without that distinction would overstate what it does — so this page states it plainly instead.

        

        

          Data, ethics & reproducibility
          
All data is synthetic, generated in your browser, and nothing is transmitted anywhere unless you explicitly enable the optional generative layer. Session data (tallies, findings, audit trail) is saved only to this browser's local storage on this device — not to any server, not synced across devices, and visible to no one else. No patients, biological specimens or human participants are involved, so this computational demonstration would not typically require research ethics approval — but that determination should still be confirmed with your institution before any results are used in a publication. Random generation is seeded: setting the session seed (Evidence page) and repeating the same actions in the same order reproduces identical practice cases, series and results. Generative explanations and server data are not reproducible by seed.

        

        

          Current limitations / roadmap
          
This single-file version does not include: a trained ML model (the optional image analysis on the Laboratory page is classical computer vision — thresholding and blob counting — not a learned model), a locked validation dataset with ground-truth labels, sensitivity/specificity/F1 benchmarking, multi-user accounts, or a persistent server-side database. Those need a real backend and are a natural next phase, not something a static HTML file run in one browser can honestly claim to do.

          External data sources — what's live, what isn't, and why
          
This project started from a plan to use real public datasets (Dataset19 on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0) and real third-party tools (AMRIE, R AMR, Cellpose). Here's exactly what a static file like this one can and can't do with each:

          
    
            
  • Dataset19 metadata — Zenodo's file API supports direct browser fetches for small files. The button below attempts a live fetch of that dataset's real record metadata, right now, in your browser.
    • 
            
  • Dataset19 images — not fetchable in practice: the real photos are bundled in one 5.6 GB archive, not separate files, so "loading a real photo" would mean your browser downloading the entire archive first. Not attempted here.
    • 
            
  • AMRIE / R AMR / Cellpose — these are software packages, not web services. No browser trick reaches them; they need a real .NET, R, or Python/GPU runtime respectively. The separate FastAPI/PostgreSQL backend project delivered earlier in this project (AMR-LabAI.zip) has real, currently-mocked-but-swappable adapters for exactly this — this single HTML file architecturally cannot.
    •

Getting started



What this app is


AMR-LEARN is a teaching and research tool for laboratory microbiology and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). It lets you practise four things: reading antimicrobial susceptibility results (S/I/R) with a transparent rule set, working out a presumptive organism identification from culture characteristics, checking MALDI-TOF scores against editable cut-offs, and exploring a research image classifier that suggests a species from a plate photograph. It also includes stewardship (antibiotic use) and knowledge pages for practice.


This is a teaching and research demonstration. It is not a medical device, is not validated for clinical use and is not for patient care. Do not enter real patient data. The footer and the bar at the top of every page repeat this. The link in that bar opens the Reliability page, which lists what the app does and does not claim.



How it runs, and what connects to the internet


The whole app is one HTML page that runs in your browser. Case generators, the rule engine, the identifier, the MALDI-TOF checker and the image model all run on your device. Practice data are synthetic and generated from a numeric seed. Your session (tallies, findings, audit trail, case log) is kept in this browser's local storage so a refresh does not lose it.


Three optional connections exist. Everything else works offline.


    

  • Optional explanation layer. On Evidence, Explanation layer, you may paste your own Anthropic API key. New laboratory interpretations are then rewritten in plain language by a language model, which can only restate the rule engine's output. The key is held in this tab's memory only. With no key the layer is off.
    • 

  • Zenodo record check. On Evidence, About, a button attempts a live fetch of the metadata of the dataset record cited by the app (Zenodo record 18256864). It only runs when you press it, and it reports plainly if the browser or network blocks it.
    • 

  • Local server. On Overview, the Server connection box can sign in to a backend server if you have one running. Without it the app says "not connected (browser demo mode)". A server can add its own rule engine, detectors and image model.
    • 




Navigating


The top navigation lists the pages: Overview, Laboratory, Stewardship, Knowledge, Reliability and Evidence. Pages with sub-tabs show a tab row under the page heading (for example Interpret, Identify, Organisms on Laboratory). Tabs can be reached from a link such as #/lab/identify, and you can use the arrow keys, Home and End to move between tabs. The address bar always shows where you are, so a link can be bookmarked.

  • Role view (the select in the header): All views, Laboratory, Infection prevention, Stewardship or Executive. It filters which domain rows and signals the Overview shows; Executive also hides the Ask and graph blocks. The setting is remembered on this device.
    • 

  • Dark mode: the round half-filled button in the header switches between light and dark and remembers your choice.
    • 

  • Search: press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac) to open search and jump to a page or topic.
    • 

  • Help: press ? or use the help button to open this manual at the section for the page you are on. Press Esc to close dialogs.
    • 

  • Sidebar: press [ to collapse or expand the sidebar.
    • 




What the disclaimer means


Output is presumptive and educational. Rule-based text says what a pattern is "compatible with"; it never confirms a mechanism. An identification from an image, a colour or a characteristic ranking must be confirmed by MALDI-TOF, biochemical tests or sequencing. Real susceptibility testing needs a grown isolate exposed to each antimicrobial. The app never predicts susceptibility from an image or from an organism name.



Related pages


Overview · Laboratory · Reliability · Evidence







Overview



What this page is for


Overview is the home page. It shows a system status line (synthetic demonstration data, the session seed), the Server connection box, and four sub-tabs: Now, Evidence, Ask and System. It collects what you have analysed elsewhere into one "current intelligence state".



How to use it


    

  1. On Now, read "Start here": three short missions (Identify a culture, Read a susceptibility result, Spot a trend). Tick the steps as you complete them and type in My notes. Ticks and notes stay on this device; Download my notes (.txt) saves them.
    2. 

  2. Run an analysis on the Laboratory or Stewardship pages. Return to Now: the "Current intelligence state" table fills in, and any moderate or high result appears under "Priority signals".
    3. 

  3. Open a signal's "Why am I seeing this?" for its evidence chain, contradicting evidence and what would confirm or refute it. Use the Status select on a signal to move it through its lifecycle, and Investigate to open an investigation (shown under "Investigations").
    4. 

  4. On Evidence, press a node in the graph (source, method, signal, investigation) to see its source, method, rule, version and confidence.
    5. 

  5. On Ask, choose one of the fixed questions, for example "Why did each signal trigger?" or "What don't we know?".
    6. 

  6. On System, press Run now beside "Software self-tests" to run the checks.
    7. 




Controls explained




Role view
Header select that limits which domains and rows are shown.


Server connection
Collapsible box. Sign in only if you run a backend; otherwise leave it.


Status (on a signal)
Lifecycle label for the signal, set by you.


Investigate
Creates an investigation record linked to the signal.





Reading the results


    

  • State pills: Not assessed (nothing run), Stable, Elevated (moderate signal), High priority (high signal).
    • 

  • Data quality is the weakest completeness across analyses; Evidence confidence is the lowest overall confidence, and is capped at moderate because mechanisms are unconfirmed and most signals come from one module.
    • 

  • Each signal card shows evidence completeness, interpretation confidence and mechanism certainty ("Not established").
    • 

  • Ask answers only from this session's evidence, with the rule ID for each claim, and does not change any signal.
    • 

  • System shows the ruleset (browser-rules-1.0), reference data (AWaRe, embedded), that surveillance data are synthetic only, the generative layer (Off unless you add a key), and that external and clinical validation are not available or not done.
    • 




Limits and cautions


All signals come from synthetic or practice data you generated. Nothing here is validated for clinical use, and nothing detects a real outbreak.



Related pages


Laboratory · Stewardship · Reliability · Evidence







Laboratory



What this page is for


Laboratory Intelligence is the main working page. It applies versioned rules to susceptibility (AST) results you enter, offers an illustrated identification exercise, an organism reference gallery, a MALDI-TOF checker, image analysis, advanced data tools, real photographs and worked cases. Each is a sub-tab with its own help section below.



How to use it


    

  1. Read the banner at the top: the module never predicts susceptibility from an image or an organism's identity alone.
    2. 

  2. Choose a sub-tab from the tab row: Interpret, Identify, Organisms, MALDI-TOF, Image analysis, Advanced, Real photographs or Worked cases.
    3. 

  3. For a first run, follow Overview mission 1 (identify a culture) and mission 2 (read a susceptibility result).
    4. 

  4. Use Print this page to print the current tab.
    5. 




Controls explained




Sub-tabs
Eight tabs. Arrow keys, Home and End move between them.


Print this page
Opens the browser print dialog for the current page.





Reading the results


Every result carries a label: rule-derived (fixed logic), statistical, generative (only if you added a key) or uncertain. An evidence ladder shows Presumptive, Supported or Confirmed; almost everything in this app stays at Presumptive.



Limits and cautions


Drawn plates are illustrations, not photographs. Organism profiles and rules are teaching material not reviewed by a microbiologist. Presumptive only; research and teaching use, not a medical device.



Related pages


Overview · Reliability · Knowledge







Laboratory: Interpret



What this page is for


Interpret has two stages. Stage A is an interactive diagram-based exercise in presumptive identification (Gram stain, culture appearance, confirmatory test). Stage B takes S/I/R results you already have and applies deterministic rules to describe the pattern. It does not do real testing and does not predict susceptibility.



How to use it


    

  1. Optional Stage A: press Receive specimen & Gram stain and answer the questions that appear (for a Gram-negative rod: lactose on MacConkey, colony appearance, then order tests such as indole, motility or oxidase). Or press Skip — I already know the organism.
    2. 

  2. In Stage B choose the Organism (auto-filled from Stage A) and the Specimen (Urine, Blood culture, Wound swab, Sputum, Rectal screen).
    3. 

  3. For each antimicrobial in the panel, set S, I or R, or leave Not tested. Or press Generate practice case for a synthetic case.
    4. 

  4. Press Analyse. Press Clear to start over.
    5. 

  5. Read the Interpretation card and the "Recent cases this session" table (the last five cases).
    6. 




Controls explained




Organism
One of the modelled organisms; the panel of antimicrobials changes with it.


Not tested
Treated as missing data, never as susceptible.


Generate practice case
Builds a synthetic scenario from the session seed; most intrinsic resistances are applied and occasionally one result is left blank.





Reading the results


    

  • Interpretation is the pattern name, for example a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales-like pattern, a possible ESBL- or AmpC-associated phenotype, an MRSA-compatible pattern, VRE-compatible, azole-resistant, or "No significant resistance detected". The rule depends on the organism group.
    • 

  • Alert level: High priority, Moderate or No alert. Three or more non-intrinsic resistances add an MDR note.
    • 

  • Interpretation confidence: High (rule matched, complete data), Moderate (partial data) or Low (contradicts expected intrinsic resistance).
    • 

  • Evidence certainty: normally "Phenotype only, not confirmed by molecular or mechanistic testing".
    • 

  • Flags explain expected intrinsic resistance (not counted as an alert), unexpected susceptibility to an intrinsically resistant drug, and untested agents. If nothing is tested the result is "Insufficient information".
    • 

  • Stewardship relevance is general text, never a drug recommendation.
    • 




Limits and cautions


Rules are loosely informed by EUCAST expert-rule concepts; breakpoints are not embedded and the rules are not clinically reviewed. If you entered a key on Evidence, a language model may restate the result, but it cannot change it. Educational output only.



Related pages


Identify · Organisms · Worked cases · Knowledge







Laboratory: Identify



What this page is for


Identify holds a collapsible tool, "Optional: identify by characteristics". You enter what you observe on plates and in tests, and the app ranks organisms in its reference set by how many characteristics agree. The label on the panel says "all 46 organisms", while the gallery on Organisms counts 69; the count may differ because only some organisms have full characteristic profiles.



How to use it


    

  1. Open the panel.
    2. 

  2. Press Mystery organism (practice) to receive a hidden organism, or skip this and enter your own observations.
    3. 

  3. Fill any of the fields in the form. They include Gram stain / microscopy, Oxidase, Catalase, Coagulase, Indole, Motility, appearance on MacConkey, blood or XLD agar, Pigment, Swarming, Germ tube, chromogenic Candida agar colour, Optochin, Bacitracin, Novobiocin, Arabinose, Endospores, Sugar utilisation, TCBS colour, Urease, and recognition on a special medium.
    4. 

  4. Read the ranking that appears under the form. Press Clear answers to start again.
    5. 




Controls explained




Mystery organism
Practice mode that hides the answer so you can reason towards it.


Clear answers
Resets every characteristic.





Reading the results


    

  • Candidates are ranked by a weighted score. Each characteristic you enter adds its weight if it agrees with the organism's profile and subtracts it if it disagrees; characteristics not recorded for an organism are ignored.
    • 

  • A level is shown: Insufficient (fewer than 3 informative characteristics), Low, Moderate, or High (no disagreement, a clear margin over the second candidate and at least 5 characteristics).
    • 

  • If nothing fits, the tool says Out of scope or inconsistent rather than naming a best guess. The Reliability page's simulation describes how often this level is right when characteristics are entered with random errors.
    • 




Limits and cautions


Profiles are teaching material not reviewed by a microbiologist. A ranking is presumptive and needs confirmation by MALDI-TOF, biochemical panels or sequencing. The reference set only holds the organisms listed in the app.



Related pages


Interpret · Organisms · MALDI-TOF · Compare organisms







Laboratory: Organisms



What this page is for


A reference library. The gallery shows every organism the simulator models (69, of which 19 have guided identification) with its plate illustration, media type and Gram category. Below it, the Organism reference lets you look up one organism and see how it looks on every plate, its characteristics, biochemical tests and antibiotic panel.



How to use it


    

  1. Click a gallery card to jump into an identification exercise for that organism.
    2. 

  2. In Search organism, type a name to open its profile. Press Enter to open the first match.
    3. 

  3. In the profile use the tabs Plates: all organisms, One plate, Susceptibility (AST) and Biochemical tests.
    4. 

  4. In the plate table, use Show group to filter (Enterobacterales, Non-fermenters, Gram-positive cocci, Gram-positive rods, Anaerobes, Fastidious organisms, Gram-negative enteric pathogens, Mycobacteria, Yeasts, Moulds). Tick Show written descriptions in the plate views for text under each dish.
    5. 

  5. Select any plate to enlarge it, or an organism name for its full profile.
    6. 




Controls explained




Show group
Limits the table to one organism group.


Plate columns
BA blood agar, CHOC chocolate, MAC MacConkey, CLED, XLD, MSA, URINE, CANDIDA, SDA, TM, TCBS, CIN, CCDA, BCYE, CCFA, TELL, BG, LJ, BIRD, SMAC, BBE; a legend under the table gives the full names.





Reading the results


An empty dish means no growth is expected on that medium. A small dot means nothing is recorded for that organism on that medium. Gallery cards marked "reference" have a plate and profile but no guided identification. Interpretation of the colours comes from the drawn illustrations only.



Limits and cautions


Images are drawn illustrations, not photographs. Descriptions and profiles are teaching material not reviewed by a microbiologist. Real colonies vary with strain, medium batch, incubation and imaging.



Related pages


Identify · Real photographs · Interpret







Laboratory: MALDI-TOF



What this page is for


Teaches how a MALDI-TOF identification score is read. You enter the instrument's reported organism and score; the app compares the score to species-level and genus-level cut-offs and checks the name against the reference set and against any characteristics you entered on Identify. It never replaces the instrument's report.



How to use it


    

  1. Choose the System: Bruker MALDI Biotyper (log score), bioMérieux VITEK MS (confidence %) or Other system. The cut-off boxes fill with starting values (Bruker species 2.0, genus 1.7; VITEK MS species 60).
    2. 

  2. Optionally enter a Sample ID. Do not use patient identifiers.
    3. 

  3. Enter the Reported organism and Score, and optionally a Second match and Second score.
    4. 

  4. Edit Species-level at or above and Genus-level at or above if your laboratory validated different values. For Other system, both must be set.
    5. 

  5. Press Check result, then Add to log to keep it. Use organism in laboratory case sends the resolved organism to Interpret.
    6. 

  6. To load many results, use Import CSV and Export log (CSV) to save the log.
    7. 




Controls explained




Score range
Bruker 0 to 3; VITEK MS 0 to 100. Out-of-range scores are rejected.


CSV columns
sample_id, organism, score, system (bruker, vitek or other), second_organism, second_score. Up to 500 rows.





Reading the results


    

  • Species-level identification: score at or above the species cut-off.
    • 

  • Genus-level only: between the genus and species cut-offs; species not reliable.
    • 

  • No reliable identification: below the genus cut-off. Cut-off not set appears if no species cut-off is entered.
    • 

  • Flags include a close second match (within 0.2 for Bruker or 10 for VITEK MS, naming a different organism), name not in the reference set, or disagreement with entered characteristics. Notes warn where MALDI-TOF cannot separate organisms (for example E. coli and Shigella).
    • 




Limits and cautions


Cut-offs are common manufacturer defaults written into the app from memory and are not verified against your instrument. Confirm them with the current instructions and your own validation. The log stays in this browser tab and is not saved. Proposed changes to cut-offs are handled under Reliability, Change control.



Related pages


Identify · Interpret · Reliability







Laboratory: Image analysis



What this page is for


Two separate tools work on a plate photograph you upload. The first, "Experimental image analysis", is classical image processing: a quality check and threshold-based blob counting. It is not a trained model. The second, "Trained-model suggestion (research only)", runs a ResNet-18 neural network in your browser that proposes a species from 19 it knows, and says "cannot tell" when it is unsure. Nothing is uploaded or stored.



How to use it


    

  1. Under What media is this a photo of? choose the medium (MacConkey, blood, CHROMagar Candida, chocolate and 17 others).
    2. 

  2. Choose a plate photo with the file input. The page reports quality (sharpness, brightness, contrast, size). If quality is "good", it detects candidate colonies and draws boxes.
    3. 

  3. Optional correction: click a box to remove it, drag on the image to add a missed colony, or press the reset button. Corrected boxes are used by the colony-crop model.
    4. 

  4. In the Trained-model card, pick Which model (shown when both are bundled): Colony crops (needs 3 or more separate colonies) or Whole plate.
    5. 

  5. Press Ask the model about this photo. It can take several seconds. Check the model shows the model card.
    6. 

  6. If you know the true organism from MALDI-TOF, sequencing or a biochemical panel, use "Record what it really was" and Save confirmation. Export run record (no image) saves a small JSON file.
    7. 

  7. Optional: use "Collect labelled colony crops" to save crops to a file on your device, and "Cited reference images" to keep a list of citations and licences (Export and Import CSV).
    8. 




Controls explained




Colony crops mode
The page cuts up to 12 well-separated colonies from the photo (each at least 24 px and under 35% of the plate width or height), resizes each to 128 px, and averages the model's probabilities. At least 3 colonies are needed or the model is not run.


Whole plate mode
The whole photo is resized to 224 px and read three times: as taken, flipped left-right and flipped top-bottom.


Confidence threshold explorer
For the whole-plate model, a teaching control showing what other thresholds would have done in cross-validation. It does not change the app.





Reading the results


    

  • Top class and probability: up to three presumptive suggestions with a score from the softmax (the network's normalised output, averaged over colonies or views). The score is not a calibrated probability of being correct. The margin over the second suggestion is shown; a small margin means more uncertainty.
    • 

  • Abstention ("Cannot tell"): in colony mode the model abstains if fewer than 70% of colonies agree on the top answer, or the averaged confidence is below 90%. In whole-plate mode it abstains unless all three views give the same top answer and the averaged confidence is at least 90%. The reason is written out.
    • 

  • Agreement is the share of colonies (or views) that agree with the top answer.
    • 

  • Calibration and reliability: the app does not draw a reliability diagram. The whole-plate card shows, from five-fold cross-validation, how often answers in a confidence band were right, plus coverage versus accuracy by threshold. Calibration error for your own predictions is on Reliability, Models and server.
    • 

  • The classical analysis also gives a colour-based hint and a list of "closest illustrated matches", which is colour distance to drawn plates only, not image recognition. Haemolysis is deliberately not estimated.
    • 




Limits and cautions


The model was trained on one hospital's photographs from one closed imaging box and knows only 19 species; it will force any other organism, medium or camera into one of them, and may partly read agar colour. It was not tested on other photo sources. The colony-crop accuracy was measured with the dataset authors' colony boxes, while this page finds colonies itself, which has not been evaluated. It never predicts susceptibility. Suggestions are presumptive and must be confirmed by MALDI-TOF, biochemical tests or sequencing. Research only; not validated for clinical use.



Related pages


Real photographs · Reliability: Models and server · MALDI-TOF







Laboratory: Advanced



What this page is for


Data tools for people who want to export the app's reference data, extend the organism set, or connect a server.



How to use it


    

  1. Open Export reference data and press Reference JSON, Biochemical table (CSV) or AST panels (CSV).
    2. 

  2. To add organisms, open Add organisms (JSON import), press Download template, fill it in, paste one organism object or an array into the box and press Validate and add. Remove custom organisms deletes what you added.
    3. 

  3. Open Server integration (API) for the list of server endpoints.
    4. 




Controls explained




Add organisms
Adds reference-only entries (plates and characteristics, no antibiotic rules). Entries are validated and stay in this browser.


Server endpoints
With a backend running: GET /reference/organisms?q=, GET /reference/organisms/{key}, POST /identify, POST /maldi/results, POST /maldi/csv, GET /maldi/results. A user with the role instrument can be created for an instrument connection, and interactive documentation is at /docs on the server.





Reading the results


Invalid JSON is rejected with a message under the box. Custom organisms appear in the identifier ranking and reference views and are marked as custom.



Limits and cautions


Added organisms have no interpretation rules, so they cannot be used for AST interpretation. Do not paste patient data. The reference data are teaching material and have not been reviewed by a microbiologist.



Related pages


Organisms · MALDI-TOF · Overview (server connection)







Laboratory: Real photographs



What this page is for


One real photograph per species from an open clinical colony-image set (Jilin set, Du and colleagues; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18256864, version 2; CC BY 4.0; photographed in a closed imaging box at the First Hospital of Jilin University). Photographs are reduced in size. It lets you practise naming a species by eye and see why look-alikes are hard.



How to use it


    

  1. Read the "Read this first" notice.
    2. 

  2. Under Practise look at the photograph, choose a species from the four options and check the answer. This is a presumptive guess.
    3. 

  3. Browse the Gallery of 19 species photographs.
    4. 

  4. Under Why is it hard? Compare look-alikes use the Streptococci, Enterobacterales and Staphylococci tabs to see species side by side.
    5. 




Controls explained




Practise options
Four species names; one is correct.


Look-alike tabs
Groups of species that resemble each other on a plate, with a note on what separates them (haemolysis pattern, Lancefield grouping, optochin or bile solubility, MALDI-TOF).





Reading the results


The practice answer tells you whether your guess matched the photograph's recorded species. A correct guess is not an identification. The look-alike notes show that agar type can change the appearance of a plate more than species does.



Limits and cautions


In this dataset most species were grown on one agar each, so plate colour and background can give the answer away. Your plates, camera and medium will look different. Naming a species from a photograph is presumptive only. The drawn plates elsewhere in the app are diagrams, not photographs. Reuse of the photographs requires CC BY attribution.



Related pages


Image analysis · Worked cases · Organisms







Laboratory: Worked cases



What this page is for


Six constructed teaching examples that join a real photograph to a susceptibility panel. They are not real patients. Each case has three steps: guess the species, read the panel, and write what would make you less sure.



How to use it


    

  1. For each case, in Step 1 choose a species (presumptive).
    2. 

  2. In Step 2 read the panel, which assumes your species label is correct, and choose the resistance pattern that fits (for example an ESBL-like pattern, a carbapenem-resistant pattern, an MRSA phenotype, a VRE phenotype or no pattern of concern).
    3. 

  3. In Step 3 type your own answer to "What would make you less sure?" and compare it with the key.
    4. 

  4. Tick Teacher mode (show keys) to reveal the answers. Use the print option to print worked cases or an answer sheet.
    5. 




Controls explained




Teacher mode (show keys)
Shows answer keys; leave it off for self-testing.


Case 6
Has no susceptibility results; the correct response is that nothing about resistance can be said.





Reading the results


The pattern choices mirror the rule engine's categories, so you can compare your reading with what Interpret would say for the same panel. Missing data produce an "it cannot be read" outcome, not a guess.



Limits and cautions


The panels are constructed for teaching. Species in the panels are assumed correct; in real work identity must be confirmed first. Nothing here predicts susceptibility from a photograph.



Related pages


Real photographs · Interpret · Knowledge







Stewardship



What this page is for


Stewardship Intelligence audits a simulated antimicrobial-use dataset (defined daily doses, DDD) against the WHO AWaRe framework (Access, Watch, Reserve). It has two sub-tabs, Audit and AWaRe reference.



How to use it


    

  1. On Audit choose an Antibiotic from the 28 listed, each labelled Access, Watch or Reserve.
    2. 

  2. Choose a Utilisation scenario: Stable, Increasing, Decreasing or Fluctuating.
    3. 

  3. Press Run audit to see the trend result and bar chart.
    4. 

  4. Press Regenerate facility dataset to draw a new dataset. The mix and every trend update together.
    5. 

  5. Read the facility AWaRe mix below and compare with the WHO target.
    6. 

  6. Use AWaRe reference to see which antibiotics are in each group.
    7. 




Controls explained




Utilisation scenario
Controls the shape of the generated 24-month series for the chosen antibiotic.


Regenerate facility dataset
Replaces the simulated dataset using the session seed.





Reading the results


    

  • The trend compares the mean of the first six months with the mean of the last six. An increase of 60% or more is "High-priority utilisation increase"; 30% to under 60% is "Rising utilisation, review"; a fall of 20% or more is "Decreasing utilisation"; otherwise there is no concern.
    • 

  • The facility mix shows Access, Watch and Reserve percentages calculated from the dataset's total DDD, and the gap to the WHO target of at least 70% Access.
    • 

  • This is a classical statistical comparison, not a trained model.
    • 




Limits and cautions


The data are simulated. The AWaRe quick reference is marked illustrative: verify against the current WHO AWaRe book. The tool never instructs starting, stopping or switching any agent, and the thresholds are teaching thresholds without clinical sign-off.



Related pages


Overview · Knowledge · Interpret







Knowledge



What this page is for


Knowledge and Practice offers difficulty-levelled practice cases, a confidence-calibration check on your own answers, a rule-engine safety benchmark, and a tool to compare two candidate organisms. The seed shown at the top controls which cases you get.



How to use it


    

  1. On Practice choose a Difficulty level (1 Basic, 2 MDR, 3 ESBL/AmpC-type, 4 Carbapenem resistance, 5 Ambiguous or partial data, 6 Contradictory data) and press Generate case.
    2. 

  2. Read the panel chips, choose the most likely resistance pattern, optionally press Get a hint, choose your confidence (Low, Moderate or High) and press Check my answer.
    3. 

  3. Read the rule engine's interpretation and stewardship note shown after you answer.
    4. 

  4. Look at "Your calibration this session" once you have answered a few cases.
    5. 

  5. Press Run safety benchmark to test the rule engine on five fixed edge cases.
    6. 

  6. On Compare organisms choose Hypothesis A and Hypothesis B, then press Compare.
    7. 




Controls explained




Get a hint
A fixed Socratic prompt for the chosen level, used before you commit.


Confidence
Your self-rating, used only for the calibration summary.





Reading the results


    

  • Calibration summary compares how often you were right at each confidence level. If high-confidence answers are not correct more often than low-confidence ones, your confidence is not yet tracking accuracy.
    • 

  • Safety benchmark reports a safe-response rate over five fixed cases (sufficient, missing and contradictory data). It covers only the rule engine, is not a live AI evaluation, and the generative layer is not benchmarked.
    • 

  • Compare organisms lists the distinguishing tests and intrinsic-resistance differences already encoded in the app. Nothing is generated.
    • 




Limits and cautions


Practice cases are synthetic. Your statistics are session-only teaching feedback. The benchmark is small and fixed.



Related pages


Interpret · Identify · Reliability







Reliability



What this page is for


Reliability states how the system checks itself and what it does not claim. Everything here uses synthetic data or your own session; none of it is clinical validation. It has six tabs: Claims, Self-checks, Feedback and drift, Review and data, Change control, and Models and server.



How to use it


    

  1. Claims: read the table of claims and their status (Tested, Simulated, Not assessed, Not validated, No).
    2. 

  2. Self-checks: see the startup self-check result (for example 80/80 passed) and press Run again. Press Run simulation for the scope-and-calibration table. "Consistency checks" lists results from this session that contradict each other.
    3. 

  3. Feedback and drift: mark results as agreeing or disagreeing using the buttons that appear under identification, laboratory and MALDI-TOF results. Show a synthetic drift example and Clear demo events help you see the drift watch.
    4. 

  4. Review and data: label queued cases, export labelled cases (JSON or CSV), clear them, and save an approval record.
    5. 

  5. Change control: propose a change to an identifier weight (0.5 to 5) or to MALDI-TOF cut-offs with a reason and your name.
    6. 

  6. Models and server: read the model card and upload a CSV under "Evaluate predictions you already have".
    7. 




Controls explained




Scope and calibration simulation
Enters characteristics with 8% random mistakes using a fixed seed and reports how often each confidence level was right. It describes behaviour, not real-world accuracy.


Drift watch
Compares the share of flagged results in the first 30 events with the latest 20, per module; needs 50 events. A shift may come from different inputs rather than a fault.


Reviewer feedback
Rates are shown only after at least 10 reviews for a group. Notes must not contain patient details.


Change control (shadow mode)
A proposal runs silently beside the current setting and can only be approved after at least 20 comparisons by a different person. It is local to this browser.


Approval record
Stored on this device and attached to exports. The app cannot check the approval.





Reading the results


    

  • The models tab shows intended use, data handling, versions (application 1.0, engine prototype 0.8, rules browser-rules-1.0, detector MA + EWMA + CUSUM, reference AWaRe), training data, known limits, and a table per model with a file fingerprint (short checksum of the weights, quote it with any kept result), cross-validated accuracy, single-split accuracy and external test status.
    • 

  • Evaluate predictions: upload a CSV with columns reference and predicted (and optional confidence from 0 to 1). You get accuracy with a 95% interval and per-class sensitivity and precision. With at least 30 confidence values, a calibration error is added: the average gap between confidence and accuracy over ten confidence bins, weighted by bin size. Fewer than 30 rows triggers a "Too few cases" warning; the first 5,000 rows are used.
    • 




Limits and cautions


The app records no real isolates tested, no independent review, no ethics approval and no external validation of the image models. Confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities. Use data you are permitted to use.



Related pages


Evidence · Image analysis · MALDI-TOF







Evidence



What this page is for


Evidence and Audit shows what the app knows about your session: tallies, the reproducibility seed, self-tests, the audit trail, the optional explanation layer and an About page that separates rule-derived, statistical and generative components.



How to use it


    

  1. Summary: see counts of cases analysed, AMR alerts, emerging signals and stewardship flags. To reproduce a session, type a number in Set a specific seed and press Use this seed, or press New random seed.
    2. 

  2. Use Export session (.json) and Import session (.json) to move a session between browsers. Clear session data on this device deletes it permanently after confirmation.
    3. 

  3. Audit trail: read the time, module, method and output for each action this session (the 50 most recent are kept) and press Export audit trail (.csv). Verify server audit trail applies when a server is connected.
    4. 

  4. Self-tests: press Run self-tests.
    5. 

  5. Explanation layer: to use it, paste your own key in Anthropic API key (optional) and press Enable for this session; Clear key removes it.
    6. 

  6. About: read what is and is not AI, the roadmap, the changelog and the external data sources. The Zenodo fetch button is here.
    7. 




Controls explained




Seed
Same seed plus the same sequence of clicks gives identical generated cases; a different order diverges.


Self-tests
Fixed checks of the rule engine, the identification logic and the seeded generator against known answers.





Reading the results


    

  • Component tags: Rule-derived (identification and AST interpretation), Statistical (moving average, EWMA, CUSUM and the stewardship trend), Generative (optional, explains only) and Uncertain (shown when evidence is missing, contradictory or outside the organism list).
    • 

  • The audit trail is session-only and not a substitute for a versioned production audit log.
    • 

  • Generative text is checked mechanically for rule IDs and numbers, not for clinical truth.
    • 




Limits and cautions


Your key is kept in this tab's memory only, but text is sent to the language model provider when it is enabled; do not include patient data. No component here is a validated clinical machine-learning classifier. The one trained model is the research image classifier on the Image analysis tab.



Related pages


Overview · Reliability · Image analysis





Figures, numbers and display options


Reading a chart
Move the pointer over a chart (or tab to it and use the left and right arrow keys) to see the value for each month in a small read-out, with a vertical guide line. Detection markers carry a text label and a different dash pattern, so they can be told apart without colour.


Exporting a figure
Under each chart, SVG saves a vector picture, PNG saves an image at three times the size, and CSV saves the plotted values as a table. Every export carries a line with the app version, the session seed, the date and the words “synthetic teaching data”, so the figure can be traced back. The CSV starts with two comment lines beginning with “#”; delete them if your software does not accept them. The CSV button is greyed out for figures that have no table of values.


Explaining a number
Click (or press Enter on) a headline number, such as the counters in the sidebar or the tiles on Trends, to open a short explanation of exactly what is counted. These counters are prompts for review, not findings.


Evidence ladder
On Reliability, Evidence and Validation, a four-step ladder shows what kind of evidence exists: rule-derived, checked on synthetic data, tested on independent real data (not established), and clinical validation (not validated). The last two steps are open on purpose.


Settings: density, contrast, Methods paragraph, what’s new
Open the gear icon. Density offers Comfortable, Compact and Presentation (larger text, fewer extras, for projecting; the disclaimer bar always stays visible). High-contrast theme strengthens borders and text colours and works with both light and dark themes. Methods paragraph writes a draft description of the current settings, version and seed that you can adapt for a report; read and edit it before use. What’s new lists the changes in each version. A red dot on the gear means there are notes you have not opened yet.


Search shortcuts
Press Ctrl K (or Cmd K) to search. With an empty search box, your last few views appear at the top under “Recent”; they are stored only in this browser and are removed by “Clear everything this app stored on this device”.





Version 1.3 additions


Detector detail and exploration (WATCH, Surveillance)
After each run, a panel under the result lists the baseline, each detector’s rule as implemented, the threshold values, the peak reached and the first month each detector signalled. A line states whether this independent recomputation agrees with the main result. Explore the settings lets you move five sliders (moving-average rise, EWMA smoothing and limit width, CUSUM slack and threshold) and see how the same series would be read. This is exploration only: the app’s defaults do not change, and one series cannot tell you which settings are better, because looser settings flag sooner but raise false alarms.


Comparing runs and sharing a run
The last eight practice series of the session are kept in memory. Compare runs plots any two on one axis, with each run’s detector results beside it. Copy link to this run makes a link that carries the 24 synthetic values, the scenario and the series, so the recipient sees the same series and results whatever their random seed. The link contains nothing else. It opens the same app file, so share it with someone who has that file or the page it is hosted on.


When the detectors go wrong (Validation)
Four constructed examples, made with a separate seeded generator and run through the app’s own detectors: a false alarm, a single-detector flag, a slow drift that is missed, and a real rise found late. They are picked to illustrate and say nothing about how often each happens.


Trends: × marks, line-list converter and export
A × on a Trends chart marks a month with no isolates (it is not plotted as zero). Convert a line list to monthly counts turns a file with one row per isolate (date, organism, antibiotic, result S/I/R) into the monthly-counts format used by the check above it. Only R counts as resistant. Rows it cannot use are counted with the reason. If there is a patient column you can keep only the first record per patient, organism, antibiotic and year. It is a basic converter that has not been tested against files from any particular laboratory system. Download all series as CSV saves the synthetic Trends data.


Calibration, mix-ups, review queue and worksheets (LEARN)
On Reliability, the calibration chart shows how often the research colony model was right within each stated-confidence band in its cross-validation, with 95% intervals, and a table lists its most frequent mix-ups. These are descriptive and not external results. On Knowledge, the Review queue brings back practice cases you answered wrongly after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days; it is stored only in this browser. Print worksheet for this case prints the current case with blank answer lines; switch on Teacher mode in Settings to add an answer-key page.


Printing
Any page now prints with a header showing the app, page, version, seed, date, a Methods paragraph and the evidence status.





Learning paths page


Three short guided routes: reading an antibiogram, colony images and their limits, and stewardship basics. Each step has an Open → link to the right page. Tick a step when you have done it; practice steps (for example “answer 3 practice cases correctly”) count automatically from the practice page. A bar shows progress, and Reset this path starts it again. Progress is stored only in this browser and is not an assessment or certificate.


Your confidence and your accuracy
Every practice answer records the confidence you chose (Low, Moderate or High) and whether you were right. The table shows how often you were right at each level with a 95% interval. If your confidence is informative, High should be right more often than Low; with few answers the intervals are wide. The last 200 answers are kept.


After a wrong answer
The practice page now adds a short note listing the resistant and intermediate results in the case, so you can see what the pattern depends on, with a link to compare organisms and a button for another case. It explains the rule engine’s answer for a teaching case, not a clinical decision.


Model card
On Reliability, under Models and server, the model card sets out what the research colony-image model is, what it is for and not for, its data, its cross-validation result and known weaknesses, with the numbers calculated from the same data as the calibration chart.




  





  
Reference
Glossary, exact definitions as implemented, data formats, shortcuts and sources for AMR-LEARN. For how to use each page, see the Manual.

  
← Back to the app



Glossary




Abstention ("cannot tell")
The image model declines to name an organism. It does so when too few colonies are found, when the views or colonies do not agree enough, or when the averaged top confidence is below its threshold. A reason is shown.


AMR
Antimicrobial resistance.


AST (antimicrobial susceptibility testing)
Laboratory testing in which a grown isolate is physically exposed to each antimicrobial. The app does not perform AST or predict it. It interprets S/I/R results that you enter or generate.


Broth microdilution
A reference AST method that gives a MIC. Named in the app as one of the two real ways to test susceptibility.


Calibration
Whether stated confidence matches how often an answer is right. It appears in three places: your own session (high versus low confidence answers on Knowledge), a simulated identifier check on Reliability, and a calibration figure for a CSV you upload. The app states that the image model's confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities.


Colony crop
A single colony cut out of a plate photo by this page's own detection, then passed to the colony-level model.


Confidence (image model)
The averaged softmax probability of the top class. It is compared with a threshold (90% for the bundled models) and is not a calibrated probability.


Coverage and accuracy by threshold
A chart in the image model panel showing accuracy when answered against the share of photographs answered, for different thresholds. It plays the role of a risk-coverage view for the model.


Cross-validation (5-fold)
Repeating training and testing five times with different held-out isolates. The model card reports the result as the isolate-held-out accuracy with an interval.


Disk diffusion
A reference AST method in which zone diameters around antibiotic disks are read. Named in the app; the app does not take zone diameters.


ECE (expected calibration error)
Reported when you upload a CSV of reference and predicted labels with confidence values (0 to 1) on Reliability. It is computed in 10 equal-width confidence bins and only when at least 30 rows have a confidence.


EUCAST expert rules
The app's interpretation logic is described as deterministic and "loosely informed by EUCAST expert-rule concepts" (for example, intrinsic resistance). EUCAST and CLSI breakpoints are not embedded.


Intrinsic resistance
Resistance expected for an organism, stored per organism in the app. It is not counted as an alert, and an unexpected S result is flagged for verification.


Isolate
One cultured organism from a specimen. Model accuracy is quoted on isolates not seen in training.


MALDI-TOF
Mass-spectrometry identification of organisms. The MALDI-TOF tab checks a result you type or import against the reference set and your cut-offs. It does not read spectra and never replaces the instrument's report.


MIC
Minimum inhibitory concentration. The app takes S/I/R categories and does not use or compute MICs.


Presumptive ID
An identification suggested but not confirmed by a reference method such as MALDI-TOF, biochemical tests or sequencing. Everything the app suggests is presumptive.


Reliability page
The page that states what the app claims and does not claim, with self-tests, drift watch, change control and the model card.


ResNet-18
The convolutional neural network architecture of the bundled image classifier. It is evaluated in plain JavaScript in your browser, with no server and no library.


S / I / R
Susceptible, Intermediate and Resistant. "Not tested" is treated as missing data, never as susceptible.


Seed (session seed)
The number driving every random generator. The same seed with the same click order reproduces the same practice cases.


Self-tests
Checks of the software and reference data that run at every page load (80 of 80 passed in the build documented here). They are not clinical validation.


Softmax
The function that turns the network's raw outputs into probabilities across the classes. Softmax outputs are averaged across views or colonies.


Top-class agreement
The share of views or colonies whose own top class is the same. The colony model needs at least 70% to agree; the whole-plate model needs all three views to agree.


View (whole-plate model)
The photo as taken, flipped left-right, and flipped top-bottom. All three are run.


Wilson interval
The 95% interval used for proportions such as accuracy.









Interpretation rules


The Interpret tab applies deterministic rules to the S/I/R results of a panel. The rules are for teaching. The app states that they have not been reviewed by a microbiologist and that EUCAST and CLSI breakpoints are not embedded.


Rule-set version labels




LabelMeaning in the app



browser-rules-1.0The ruleset loaded in the browser. The final number is a revision counter: approved change-control proposals raise it (for example browser-rules-1.1).


engine prototype 0.8The engine version shown on System and in exports.


detector MA + EWMA + CUSUMThe detector set used by the practice surveillance series.


reference AWaRe (embedded)The antibiotic reference list.


Application 1.0The app release.





Rule categories




Rule IDWhat it does



LAB-001Carbapenem-resistant phenotype: an Enterobacterales isolate with meropenem R. Mechanism is not confirmed.


LAB-002ESBL-like phenotype: third-generation cephalosporin R with meropenem S in Enterobacterales.


LAB-003MRSA phenotype: S. aureus with cefoxitin R.


LAB-004VRE phenotype: Enterococcus with vancomycin R.


LAB-010Other organism-specific teaching rules that run only in the browser (for example Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Candida and coagulase-negative staphylococci).


none (insufficient data)With no usable results the app reports insufficient information.





Each interpretation gives a pattern, an alert level (high, moderate or none) and a statement that the mechanism needs confirmation. Intrinsic resistance is shown as expected, and unexpected susceptibility to an intrinsically resistant agent is flagged to verify identification and repeat testing. Clicking a rule ID shows its name, description, version and reference.


Rules for 27 of the 46 organisms with a laboratory panel were added without clinical review, and the 19 organisms with guided identification are the original set. The organism gallery lists 69 organisms in total.


Other rule IDs appear in the registry and in the Ask and Evidence views: SURV-001 (detector concordance, used in practice surveillance), STEW-001 (utilisation trend), INT-001, TEMP-001, DQ-001 (fewer than 30 isolates), DQ-002 (more than 20% of isolates without a result) and DUP-001 (first isolate per patient within 30 days). Only the LAB rules interpret panels on this edition's Laboratory page.







Image classifier


The only trained model in the app is the image classifier on Laboratory, Image analysis. It is a research demonstration that suggests an organism. It cannot change any rule-based result and no other module uses it. The rest of the page (quality check, blob counting, colour-based suggestion) is classical image processing, not a trained model.




ItemAs the app states it



ArchitectureResNet-18, run in plain JavaScript in your browser. Weights are stored as 16-bit numbers and the result is stated to match PyTorch to within 1e-6 on test tensors.


Where it runsOn your device. The photo is not uploaded and not stored.


Crop modesColony crops: needs 3 or more separate colonies and reads up to 12, cut out by this page's detection (including your corrections). It needs at least 70% of colonies to agree on one class and an averaged confidence of at least 90%. Whole plate: three views of one image (as taken, flipped left-right, flipped top-bottom). All three must give the same top class and the averaged confidence must reach 90%.


Input size128 px for the colony-crop model, as stated on its model card.


OutputUp to the top three classes with their averaged softmax confidence and the margin over the second, or "cannot tell".


Classes19 species of the Jilin colony set. The classes of each bundled model are listed in its model file.


Training dataJilin clinical colony set (Du et al., Sci Data 2026; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18256864; CC BY 4.0): 19 species, 151 isolates, 950 photographs, one hospital, one closed imaging box. The colony-crop model was trained on single colonies cut out with the authors' boxes and is the model of cross-validation fold 0 (about 60% of isolates).





Reported validation




ModelFive-fold, isolates not seenSingle splitExternal test



Colony crops (fingerprint 5346fb99)95% (92% to 97%)82% of single coloniesNone


Whole plate (fingerprint 84f0660c)76% (69% to 83%)79% of photographsNone





The fingerprint is a short checksum of the model weights. Quote it with any result you keep.


Limits stated by the app. One hospital, one imaging setup and 19 species. Species were mostly plated on one agar each, so agar appearance may account for part of the accuracy. Confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities. The colony-crop accuracy was measured with the dataset authors' colony boxes; this page finds colonies itself, which has not been evaluated. The model assigns any photograph to one of its classes and does not detect an unfamiliar medium or organism. Not tested on other labs, cameras or species. Not validated for clinical use.







Data, inputs and exports


Accepted inputs


    

  • S/I/R panels: entered by hand or generated as a seeded practice case. Fields left as Not tested are missing, never susceptible.
    • 

  • Plate photographs: any browser-readable image (the file input accepts image/*). Processed in the browser only.
    • 

  • MALDI-TOF results: typed, or imported from CSV with the columns sample_id, organism, score, system (bruker, vitek or other), second_organism, second_score. Up to 500 rows. The log stays in the browser tab and is not saved.
    • 

  • Evaluation CSV (Reliability): reference and predicted labels, with optional confidence from 0 to 1, giving accuracy with intervals, per-class sensitivity and calibration. Fewer than 30 rows are flagged as unreliable.
    • 

  • Session JSON: a session exported earlier, to load on another device or browser.
    • 



Exports


    

  • Session (.json), audit trail (.csv), and your mission notes (.txt).
    • 

  • MALDI-TOF log (.csv).
    • 

  • Image run record (.json): model, rule used, thresholds and outcome. It holds no image data.
    • 

  • Labelled colony crops, cited reference images list (.csv), labelled review cases (.json and .csv) and reviewer feedback (.csv), where you have created them.
    • 

  • Print this page, on the Laboratory and Evidence pages.
    • 



The session is saved only in this browser's local storage. Nothing is sent anywhere, and clearing it removes it from the device. Do not enter real patient data.







Real photographs


The Real photographs tab shows one photograph per species from the open Jilin clinical colony-image set (Du and colleagues; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18256864, version 2; CC BY 4.0), photographed in a closed imaging box at the First Hospital of Jilin University. Images are reduced in size. It offers a "which species is this?" practice quiz and a gallery. Marks are against the dataset label and are a presumptive guess only.


The drawn plates elsewhere in the app are teaching diagrams, not photographs.


In this dataset most species were grown on one agar each, so plate colour and background can give the answer away. Your own plates, camera and medium will look different.


Attribution. Images from the CDC Public Health Image Library (PHIL) are credited to the CDC and the contributor, and reuse needs that attribution. The classifier is not claimed to be trained on them. Its stated training data is the Jilin set above. The app's cited-reference list stores a citation, a link and a licence, not the picture, and reuse of a picture is allowed only where its licence permits.

Photograph credits
The built-in Real photographs come from the open Jilin clinical colony-image set (Du and colleagues; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18256864, version 2; CC BY 4.0), reduced in size. Any photographs added through cdc_photos.js (for example from the CDC Public Health Image Library) are listed below with the credit line supplied for each image.
No additional photographs are installed.


Evidence ladder
The ladder shows four levels of evidence and which have been reached. Level 1 means the logic follows published rules and the exact definitions in this Reference. Level 2 means it has been checked on synthetic data (regression tests and planted signals). Level 3, testing on independent real laboratory data, is not established. Level 4, evidence that use improves care, is not validated. Nothing here should be read as clinical or public-health evidence.


Typeface, colours and icons
Text is set in the Inter typeface (Rasmus Andersson and The Inter Project Authors; SIL Open Font Licence 1.1), embedded in the file so the app works offline. Chart colours for the EWMA and CUSUM markers use the Okabe and Ito colour-blind-safe palette (Okabe M, Ito K. Color Universal Design, 2008); the markers also differ by dash pattern and carry text labels, so colour is never the only cue. The logo and icons were drawn for this application.



Accessibility and keyboard shortcuts
What has been done: every page can be used from the keyboard; Ctrl K (or Cmd K) opens search; [ collapses the sidebar; Esc closes dialogs and pop-ups; focus outlines are visible; charts can be read with the left and right arrow keys; headline numbers open an explanation with Enter or Space. Chart markers differ by dash pattern and text label as well as colour, and the EWMA and CUSUM colours are colour-blind-safe. A high-contrast theme and a presentation size are in Settings, and animation is reduced when the system asks for it.
What has not been done: no formal accessibility audit and no testing with screen readers, so conformance to WCAG is not claimed. Testing was in a current Chromium browser at phone, tablet and desktop widths. Please report any barrier you find.



Trusted external resources


Official surveillance, data and teaching resources are listed here in one place so you do not have to hunt for them. These are plain links. Nothing from these sites is copied into this application, nothing is loaded from them while you use it, and no data you enter is sent to them. Each link opens in a new tab on the organisation's own website, under its own terms. This application is independent: it is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by any organisation listed, and a listing is a pointer, not a recommendation or a statement of their view. Links were checked by web search on 18 November 2026; addresses can change, so use each organisation's own search if one fails.




World Health Organization


    

  • GLASS resource centre: the Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System, with reports and guidance.
    • 

  • The WHO AWaRe antibiotic book: Access, Watch and Reserve guidance on antibiotic use.
    • 



US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention


    

  • Antimicrobial Resistance and Patient Safety Portal: hospital resistance data from the National Healthcare Safety Network.
    • 

  • Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Reports.
    • 



European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control


    

  • EARS-Net: the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network, with annual reports and data.
    • 



Laboratory standards and software


    

  • EUCAST: breakpoints and susceptibility-testing documents.
    • 

  • WHONET: free microbiology laboratory database software from the WHO Collaborating Centre for Surveillance of Antimicrobial Resistance.

Not listed: other national and regional sources. Resistance data from these sites are collected under their own methods and are not comparable with the simulated data in this application.
